Region: Alexandria, Egypt
History: Alexandria was the great Hellenistic city of Egypt, founded by Alexander. Men of the synagogue of the Alexandrians disputed with Stephen, and Apollos, eloquent in the Scriptures, came from Alexandria to Ephesus.
Culture: A centre of learning and philosophy, and home of Greek-speaking Judaism — the Septuagint, the Greek Old Testament, was produced there.
Religion: A large Jewish community alongside pagan temples; Alexandrian Judaism shaped the Greek-speaking church.
BibleConnection: Alexandrians appear as Stephen's disputants and as the home community of Apollos, whose preaching Paul and Priscilla and Aquila corrected and encouraged.

TimePeriod: c. 2000-700 BC, from Abraham's day to Hezekiah's reign
Region: The Negev, the Sinai wilderness, and the southern borders of Canaan, ranging at times into the hill country
History: The Amalekites appear as early as Genesis 14:7, in the days of Abraham, and Genesis 36:12 traces Amalek to Eliphaz son of Esau. They attacked Israel at Rephidim after the exodus (Exodus 17:8-16), where Moses' raised hands decided the battle; Balaam's oracle called Amalek 'the first of the nations' (Numbers 24:20); and Deuteronomy 25:17-19 commanded Israel to remember how they struck the stragglers and to blot out their remembrance. Saul's failure to destroy them cost him the kingdom (1 Samuel 15), David destroyed the raiders who burned Ziklag (1 Samuel 30), and a remnant was wiped out in Hezekiah's days (1 Chronicles 4:43).
Culture: Nomadic raiders of the southern desert, striking the weak and the rear of a marching people, then vanishing into the wilderness. They lived by plunder rather than by cities.
Religion: The text describes no Amalekite religion in detail; their defining mark in the Bible is hostility to Israel, from Rephidim to Haman's later line (Esther 3:1 traces Haman to Agag).
BibleConnection: Amalek is Israel's standing enemy: the first nation to make war on Israel after the exodus, the test of Saul's obedience, and the target of David's vengeance at Ziklag.
KeyScriptures: Genesis 14:7; Exodus 17:8-16; Numbers 24:20; Deuteronomy 25:17-19; 1 Samuel 15:1-9; 1 Samuel 30:1-18
RelatedPeople: Moses; Joshua; King Saul; King David; Amalek; Esau
RelatedEvents: The Twelve Spies and Israel's Unbelief

Region: The hill country of Canaan and Transjordan, including the kingdoms of Sihon at Heshbon and Og at Bashan
History: The Amorites were one of the major peoples of Canaan. In Genesis 15:16 the LORD tells Abram that his descendants will return to the land when 'the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet full,' naming the Amorites for the land's peoples as a whole. In Numbers 21, Sihon king of the Amorites refused Israel passage and was defeated, and Og king of Bashan was defeated likewise, giving Israel its first Transjordan territory. Amos 2:9-10 recalls them as a people tall as cedars and strong as oaks, destroyed before Israel. Amorite names also appear widely in Mesopotamian records of the period.
Culture: A Semitic people who moved from a pastoral life into cities and kingdoms across the Levant and Mesopotamia. In Canaan they held fortified hill-country towns and, east of the Jordan, organized kingdoms with kings, armies, and walled cities such as Heshbon.
Religion: They shared the religious world of Bronze Age Canaan, worshipping the gods of the Canaanite pantheon. The Bible presents their worship as part of the idolatry Israel was commanded to reject.
BibleConnection: The Amorites are the standing example of the peoples whose land Israel inherited: named in the promise to Abram, defeated in the wilderness, listed among the seven nations to be driven out, and remembered by the prophets as proof of God's judgment and gift.
KeyScriptures: Genesis 15:16; Genesis 15:21; Numbers 21:21-35; Deuteronomy 1:27; Deuteronomy 7:1; Amos 2:9-10
RelatedEvents: The Twelve Spies and Israel's Unbelief

TimePeriod: Wilderness and conquest era, c. 1400-1200 BC
Region: The hill country of Judah (Hebron, Debir, Anab) and, after the conquest, Gaza, Gath, and Ashdod
History: The Anakim descended from Anak (Numbers 13:33; Deuteronomy 9:2). The spies reported them as giants: 'we were in our own sight as grasshoppers, and so we were in their sight' (Numbers 13:33). Joshua cut them off from the hill country, leaving a remnant only in Gaza, Gath, and Ashdod (Joshua 11:21-22). Caleb drove out Sheshai, Ahiman, and Talmai, the children of Anak, from Hebron (Joshua 15:13-14), and Judges 1:20 records Caleb's taking of Hebron from the three sons of Anak.
Culture: A tall, formidable hill people whose walled towns and stature terrified the spies. Their cities in the hill country were the strongholds Caleb claimed by faith.
Religion: No distinct Anakim religion is described; they belong to the Canaanite world whose idolatry Israel was told to reject.
BibleConnection: The Anakim are the giants of the spies' report and of Caleb's faith: the very people Israel feared became the inheritance of the one spy who trusted God.
KeyScriptures: Numbers 13:28; Numbers 13:33; Deuteronomy 9:2; Joshua 11:21-22; Joshua 15:13-14; Judges 1:20
RelatedEvents: The Twelve Spies and Israel's Unbelief

Region: The Arabian Peninsula and the Syrian desert fringe
History: Arabians were the nomadic herders and caravan traders of the desert between Mesopotamia and Egypt. Kings of Arabia brought tribute to Solomon (1 Kings 10:15), Arabians raided Judah in Jehoram's reign (2 Chronicles 21:16) and joined the opposition to Nehemiah's wall under Geshem the Arabian (Nehemiah 2:19; 4:7), and Arabians were among the peoples who heard the gospel at Pentecost (Acts 2:11). Paul went away into Arabia after his conversion (Galatians 1:17).
Culture: Arabians lived by herding and by the caravan trade in incense, spices, and goods moving between Yemen, Mesopotamia, and the Mediterranean, organized in tribes under sheikhs.
Religion: Arabians worshipped pre-Islamic deities of the desert, including Al-Lat and Al-Uzza, alongside the astral gods of the caravan cities.
BibleConnection: Isaiah's oracle, the burden upon Arabia (Isaiah 21:13), and Jeremiah's list of Arabia's kings (Jeremiah 25:24) set Arabia among the nations judged with Judah's neighbors, while Pentecost and Paul's journey make Arabia part of the gospel's early geography.
KeyScriptures: 1 Kings 10:15; Isaiah 21:13; Jeremiah 25:24; Ezekiel 27:21; Nehemiah 2:19; Acts 2:11; Galatians 1:17

Region: Canaan (later Arka, on the Phoenician coast, is the common identification)
History: The Arkites are named in the Table of Nations as descendants of Canaan (Genesis 10:17; 1 Chronicles 1:15), with no further biblical history. The later Phoenician coastal town of Arka in northern Lebanon is commonly identified with them, but the text itself does not make that connection.
Culture: Nothing is recorded of Arkite culture beyond their place in the Canaanite family list; the later Arka was a Phoenician coastal town.
Religion: Nothing distinct is recorded of Arkite religion.
BibleConnection: The Arkites appear only in the Table of Nations, one branch of Canaan's family spread abroad after Babel.

Region: The island city of Arvad, off the Phoenician coast
History: The Arvadites, descendants of Canaan (Genesis 10:18; 1 Chronicles 1:16), were the people of Arvad, an island city off the Phoenician coast. Ezekiel pictures Arvad's men as Tyre's mariners and as soldiers on Tyre's walls (Ezekiel 27:8, 11) — seafarers in the service of the great trading city.
Culture: Arvadites were seafarers and shipbuilders, manning Tyre's fleets and garrisoning its walls.
Religion: As a Phoenician city, Arvad shared the religion of the Phoenician coast; nothing distinct is recorded of Arvadite worship.
BibleConnection: Arvad's biblical footprint is maritime: the island people whose sailors and soldiers powered Tyre's trade and defense.

Region: Northern Mediterranean coast, from Carmel toward Tyre and Sidon
History: Asher was Jacob's eighth son, by Leah's servant Zilpah. His name means happy, and Jacob blessed him with rich food and royal delicacies (Genesis 49:20). Asher's allotment ran along the northern coast, but the tribe never drove out the Canaanites of its towns (Judges 1:31-32) and lived among them. Asher is the quietest tribe in the history: it appears in the census lists and in the blessing of Moses (Deuteronomy 33:24-25), and Anna the prophetess, who recognised the infant Jesus in the temple, was of the tribe of Asher (Luke 2:36). The tribe was deported with the northern kingdom.
Culture: Asher's culture was coastal: farming the fertile plain, trading with the Phoenician cities to its north, and living alongside Canaanite neighbours its armies never displaced.
Religion: Asher shared Israel's worship of the LORD, though living among Canaanite towns exposed it to the idolatry the conquest was meant to remove.
BibleConnection: Asher's story is one of quiet persistence: a tribe that never produced a judge or a king, yet is named among the sealed in Revelation 7 and gives the New Testament its aged prophetess Anna.
RelatedPeople: Asher; Jacob; Moses; Joshua; Serah; Beriah; Heber; Anna the Prophetess

Region: Ava, in Mesopotamia
History: The Avites were one of the Mesopotamian peoples Assyria resettled in Samaria after Israel's fall (2 Kings 17:24). They made Nibhaz and Tartak their gods (2 Kings 17:31). They are not the Avvim of Deuteronomy 2:23, a different people near Gaza displaced by the Caphtorim — the similar names cover two different groups.
Culture: As a Mesopotamian people, the Avites shared the urban culture of Babylon's world; nothing further is recorded of them.
Religion: The Avites worshipped Nibhaz and Tartak, gods they carried with them to Samaria.
BibleConnection: The Avites appear only in the resettlement list and its note on their gods — one more strand in the mixed population that became Samaria.

Region: The southwestern coastal plain around Gaza, in unwalled settlements (Hazerim)
History: The Avvim dwelt in Hazerim, unwalled villages, on the coastal plain toward Gaza, until the Caphtorim came out of Caphtor, destroyed them, and dwelt in their place (Deuteronomy 2:23). Joshua 13:3 still counts the Avvim among the land yet to be taken, listed beside the five lords of the Philistines, a sign that a remnant remained into the conquest era.
Culture: Villagers of the coastal plain, living in unwalled settlements rather than fortified cities, which left them exposed to the Caphtorim who displaced them.
Religion: Not described in the text.
BibleConnection: The Avvim are a small, displaced people of the coast: an example in Deuteronomy 2 of how peoples rose and fell in the land before Israel ever arrived.

Region: The central hill country between Judah and Ephraim, including Jerusalem's northern approach
History: Benjamin was Jacob's youngest son, by Rachel, who died bearing him; Jacob called him son of his right hand (Genesis 35:18), and Moses' blessing pictured him dwelling safely beside the LORD (Deuteronomy 33:12). Benjamin's small allotment sat between Judah and Ephraim and included Jerusalem's northern approaches, Gibeah, Mizpah, and Bethel. The tribe nearly destroyed itself in the civil war over Gibeah (Judges 19–21). Saul, Israel's first king, was a Benjamite, and after the kingdom divided Benjamin stayed with Judah. Paul the apostle was of the tribe of Benjamin (Philippians 3:5).
Culture: Benjamin's culture was that of a small, fierce border tribe: its men were famed as left-handed slingers and archers, and its towns guarded the passes between north and south.
Religion: Benjamin shared Israel's worship of the LORD, and its territory held some of Israel's oldest sanctuaries, including Bethel and, later, the Jerusalem temple on its border with Judah.
BibleConnection: Benjamin's story runs from near-annihilation to the apostle to the Gentiles: the smallest tribe gave Israel its first king and, centuries later, Paul.
KeyScriptures: Genesis 35:18; Genesis 49:27; Deuteronomy 33:12; Joshua 18:11-28; Judges 20:1-3; 1 Samuel 9:1-2; Philippians 3:5
RelatedPeople: Benjamin; Jacob; Joseph, Son of Jacob; Moses; Joshua; Jonathan; King Saul; Ehud, Son of Gera; Mordecai; Queen Esther; Paul; Kish, Son of Abiel

Region: Caphtor (commonly identified with Crete) and, after migration, the Gaza coast
History: The Caphtorim descended from Mizraim in the table of nations (Genesis 10:14). Deuteronomy 2:23 records their migration: 'the Caphtorims, which came forth out of Caphtor, destroyed the Avvims, which dwelt in Hazerim, even unto Azzah, and dwelt in their stead.' Jeremiah 47:4 calls the Philistines 'the remnant of the country of Caphtor,' and Amos 9:7 says God brought the Philistines from Caphtor as He brought Israel from Egypt. The Caphtorim are thus closely linked to Philistine origins, but they are distinct from the Philistines themselves in the Genesis 10 list, where the Philistim come from the Casluhim. Caphtor is usually identified with Crete.
Culture: A seafaring people of Caphtor who migrated to the Gaza coast and displaced its villagers, bringing Aegean connections to the coastal plain.
Religion: No distinct Caphtorim religion is described; their Philistine kin worshipped Dagon and other coastal gods.
BibleConnection: The Caphtorim explain how the Gaza coast changed hands before Israel arrived, and Amos uses their migration as a mirror of Israel's own exodus.

Region: Eastern Asia Minor (Cappadocia)
History: Cappadocia was an inland region of Asia Minor, a Roman province by New Testament times. Cappadocians are named among the hearers at Pentecost, and Peter addresses his first letter to believers scattered through Cappadocia.
Culture: A rural, volcanic plateau; Greek-speaking under Roman rule, with Persian-era roots in its older history.
Religion: Pagan cults before conversion; by the time of 1 Peter there were Christian communities scattered through the region.
BibleConnection: Named among the peoples who heard the apostles at Pentecost, and named again among the recipients of 1 Peter.

Region: Southeastern Asia Minor (Cilicia)
History: Cilicia was the coastal region of southeastern Asia Minor, home of Tarsus. Men from the synagogue of the Cilicians disputed with Stephen, and Paul — a Cilician by birth — travelled through Cilicia strengthening the churches.
Culture: Greek-Roman cities; Tarsus was a noted centre of learning, and Paul calls himself a citizen of no mean city.
Religion: Pagan cults alongside a Jewish community strong enough to have its own synagogue in Jerusalem.
BibleConnection: Cilicians appear as Stephen's disputants and as Paul's home people; the letter of the Jerusalem Council was addressed to the brethren in Cilicia as well as Syria.

Region: Island of Crete
History: Crete was a large Mediterranean island under Roman rule. Cretans are named among the hearers at Pentecost; Paul left Titus in Crete to appoint elders in every city, and his ship to Rome sheltered at the island.
Culture: Seafaring islanders; Paul quotes a Cretan prophet's proverb about Cretans, which he applies to the false teachers troubling the island's churches.
Religion: Pagan cults before conversion; by Titus's time there were churches in every Cretan city needing elders.
BibleConnection: Cretans appear at Pentecost and as the people among whom Titus worked; Paul's letter to Titus is written to that island mission.

Region: Mesopotamia (exact site debated)
History: The Cuthites were one of the Mesopotamian peoples Assyria resettled in Samaria after Israel's fall (2 Kings 17:24). The men of Cuth made Nergal their god (2 Kings 17:30). Later Jewish tradition called the Samaritans Cuthites or Cutheans after them, though the biblical text itself does not use that name for the Samaritans.
Culture: As a Mesopotamian people, the men of Cuth shared the urban, scribal, and idol-making culture of Babylon's world.
Religion: The men of Cuth worshipped Nergal, god of the underworld and of plague, whom they set up in Samaria.
BibleConnection: The Cuthites' biblical footprint is the resettlement: a foreign people planted in Israel's empty cities, whose god Nergal joined the mixed worship of the new Samaria.

Region: Island of Cyprus
History: Cyprus was a Mediterranean island under Roman rule. Barnabas was a Cypriot by birth; men of Cyprus were among the first to preach to Greeks at Antioch; and Paul's first missionary journey began on Cyprus.
Culture: Greek-speaking islanders; Cyprus was famed for copper, from which it takes its name.
Religion: Pagan temples alongside a Jewish community; early Christian preaching reached the island on the first journey.
BibleConnection: Barnabas's homeland; Cyprus was evangelised at the start of the first missionary journey, and Cypriot believers helped found the church at Antioch.

Region: Cyrenaica, North Africa (Cyrene)
History: Cyrene was a Greek city in North Africa with a large Jewish community. Cyrenians are named among the hearers at Pentecost; Simon of Cyrene was compelled to carry Jesus' cross; and men of Cyrene preached to Greeks at Antioch.
Culture: A Greek city with a strong Jewish community, closely tied to Alexandria and to Jerusalem.
Religion: A Jewish synagogue community; Cyrenian believers were among the founders of the Gentile church at Antioch.
BibleConnection: Simon of Cyrene's part in the crucifixion and the Cyrenians' preaching at Antioch are their main New Testament appearances.

Region: Originally the central coastal plain; later the far north at Laish (Dan)
History: Dan was Jacob's fifth son, by Rachel's servant Bilhah. Jacob's blessing pictured Dan as a serpent by the roadside (Genesis 49:17). The tribe's first allotment on the coastal plain proved too small and too exposed, so part of the tribe migrated north and captured Laish, renaming it Dan (Judges 18) — the town that became proverbial as Israel's northern border, 'from Dan to Beersheba'. Samson, Israel's most famous judge, was a Danite. Under Jeroboam, Dan became one of the two sites of a golden calf (1 Kings 12:28-30). The tribe was deported with the northern kingdom by Assyria. Dan is the one tribe absent from the sealing list in Revelation 7.
Culture: Danite culture combined coastal farming with the frontier life of a border tribe; its northern city guarded the road into Israel from Syria, and its southern settlements lived among the Philistines.
Religion: Dan shared Israel's worship of the LORD, but its history is marked by two corruptions of it: Micah's shrine with its Levite priest (Judges 17–18) and Jeroboam's golden calf at Dan, which the prophets condemned.
BibleConnection: Dan illustrates both halves of the judges period: a deliverer in Samson and, in the same tribe's story, the spread of idolatry from Micah's household shrine to a royal sanctuary.
KeyScriptures: Genesis 30:6; Genesis 49:16-17; Judges 13:2; Judges 18:1-2; Judges 18:27-29; 1 Kings 12:28-30
RelatedPeople: Dan; Jacob; Samson; Delilah; Manoah, Father of Samson; Aholiab

Region: The plain later held by Moab, east of the Dead Sea
History: The Emim were an ancient people of the Moabite plain, remembered as giants. Chedorlaomer defeated them at Shaveh Kiriathaim (Genesis 14:5), and Deuteronomy 2:10-11 explains that the Emim 'were a people great, and many, and tall, as the Anakims; which also were accounted giants, as the Anakims.' The Moabites, descended from Lot, inherited the land the Emim had held.
Culture: Known only as a great and tall people of the plain, counted among the Rephaim in Deuteronomy's reckoning.
Religion: Not described in the text.
BibleConnection: The Emim belong to Deuteronomy's lesson that the land's history is a history of displacements: giants held Moab's plain before Moab, just as the Anakim held Canaan before Israel.

Region: Central hill country, Shechem and Shiloh
History: Ephraim was Joseph's younger son, adopted by Jacob as a full tribal ancestor (Genesis 48). Jacob deliberately crossed his hands to bless Ephraim above his elder brother Manasseh (Genesis 48:17-20). Ephraim's allotment covered the central hill country, including Shechem and Shiloh, where the tabernacle stood. Joshua was an Ephraimite, and the tribe's pride and power made it the leading tribe of the north: after the kingdom divided, 'Ephraim' became shorthand for the whole northern kingdom, and the prophets use the name that way (Hosea 7:8). Samaria, the northern capital, stood in Ephraim's hills. The kingdom fell to Assyria in 722 BC.
Culture: Ephraim's culture was that of the central highlands: hill farming, the sanctuary at Shiloh, and the political weight of the largest and most influential northern tribe.
Religion: Ephraim shared Israel's worship of the LORD, centred first on the tabernacle at Shiloh, but after the division its kings set up rival sanctuaries at Bethel and Dan, which the prophets condemned.
BibleConnection: Ephraim embodies the younger son chosen over the elder — and the northern kingdom's rise and fall: from Joshua's tribe to Hosea's wayward namesake, still addressed by God as 'my dear son' (Jeremiah 31:20).
KeyScriptures: Genesis 41:52; Genesis 48:17-20; Joshua 16:5-10; Judges 8:1-3; 1 Kings 12:25; Hosea 7:8
RelatedPeople: Ephraim; Jacob; Joseph, Son of Jacob; Manasseh; Moses; Joshua; Samuel; Deborah; Jeroboam; Abdon, Son of Hillel
RelatedEvents: The Kingdom Divides; Fall of Samaria

Region: East of the Jordan, Gilead from the Arnon to the Jabbok
History: Gad was Jacob's seventh son, by Leah's servant Zilpah. Jacob blessed him as a troop that would be raided and would raid in return (Genesis 49:19). Like Reuben, Gad asked Moses for Transjordan pasture land (Numbers 32) and settled Gilead. Gadites were famed as warriors: eleven Gadite captains joined David in the wilderness (1 Chronicles 12:8-15), and Gad's territory bore the brunt of Syrian and Ammonite attacks. The Mesha Stele, Moab's own record, says Gad had long dwelt in the land of Ataroth. Gad was deported with the other Transjordan tribes by Tiglath-Pileser (1 Chronicles 5:26).
Culture: Gad's culture was that of a warrior-pastoral frontier tribe, raising flocks in Gilead and manning the eastern border against Moab, Ammon, and Syria.
Religion: Gad shared Israel's worship of the LORD, with its religious life centred on the sanctuary across the Jordan; its territory included towns with altars and, later, the worship centres of the east.
BibleConnection: Gad embodies the Transjordan bargain: land east of the Jordan in exchange for fighting alongside the other tribes for Canaan, a bargain its warriors honoured from Moses to David.
RelatedPeople: Gad; Jacob; Moses; Joshua; Heber, Son of Gad's House

Region: Central Asia Minor (Galatia)
History: Celtic tribes that invaded Asia Minor settled in the central highlands and gave the region its name; under Rome it became the province of Galatia. Paul evangelised its churches on his missionary journeys and wrote them his sharpest letter.
Culture: Celtic heritage under Greco-Roman rule; by New Testament times the Galatians were Greek-speaking provincials, organised in the churches Paul founded.
Religion: Pagan Celtic and Greek cults before conversion; Paul's letter confronts Galatian believers who were turning back to law-observance as the ground of acceptance with God.
BibleConnection: Paul's letter to the Galatians defends justification by faith alone and is addressed to churches he had visited; the churches of Galatia also contributed to the collection for Jerusalem.

TimePeriod: Bronze Age, before and during the conquest
Region: Canaan (their exact territory is not stated in the text)
History: The Girgashites are listed among the sons of Canaan in Genesis 10:16, named in the land promise of Genesis 15:21, counted among the seven nations in Deuteronomy 7:1, and named among the peoples to be driven out before Israel in Joshua 3:10 and Joshua 24:11. Beyond these conquest lists, the Bible records nothing more about them: no king, city, or territory is named for them.
Culture: Unknown beyond their place among the Canaanite peoples of the conquest lists.
Religion: Unknown beyond their place among the peoples whose idolatry Israel was told to reject.
BibleConnection: The Girgashites are a reminder of how little the record preserves about some peoples: they are named in every great list of the land's nations, yet leave no story of their own.

Region: Hamath on the Orontes, in Syria
History: The Hamathites, descendants of Canaan (Genesis 10:18; 1 Chronicles 1:16), were the people of Hamath, a Syrian kingdom on the Orontes. Hamath's people were among those Assyria resettled in Samaria (2 Kings 17:24), and the kings of Hamath were named by Assyria's king when he mocked the gods of the nations (2 Kings 18:34; 19:13).
Culture: Hamath was an Aramean city-state of farmers and traders on the Orontes, a stopping point between Mesopotamia and the Mediterranean.
Religion: The men of Hamath made Ashima their god (2 Kings 17:30), and carried that worship with them to Samaria.
BibleConnection: Hamath's story in the Bible runs from the Table of Nations to the Assyrian resettlement: a Canaanite people who became a Syrian kingdom and then exiles in Israel's land.

Region: Central and northern Canaan: Shechem, Gibeon, and the region toward Lebanon and Mount Hermon
History: The Hivites are listed among the sons of Canaan in Genesis 10:17. Hamor the Hivite was the prince of Shechem in the Dinah affair (Genesis 34:2). The Gibeonites, who tricked Israel into a covenant in Joshua 9, are identified as Hivites in Joshua 9:7; their cities Gibeon, Chephirah, Beeroth, and Kirjath-jearim were spared and made woodcutters and water drawers for the congregation. They are named among the seven nations in Deuteronomy 7:1 and among the peoples left to test Israel in Judges 3.
Culture: A city-based people of central Canaan. The Gibeonite cities were organized enough to send a delegation and negotiate a treaty, and their servitude in Israel's service lasted for generations.
Religion: They shared the Canaanite religion. The Gibeonites' treaty brought them under Israel's protection, and their service was attached to the sanctuary.
BibleConnection: Hivites appear at two turning points: the violence at Shechem in Jacob's day, and the Gibeonite treaty that taught Israel the cost of a hasty oath in Joshua's day.

TimePeriod: Patriarchal era, before Esau's descendants took Seir
Region: Mount Seir (later Edom) and its mountains
History: The Horites (also called Horim) were the earlier inhabitants of Seir. Chedorlaomer defeated them in Mount Seir in Genesis 14:6, and Genesis 36:20-30 gives the genealogy of Seir the Horite and his sons: Lotan, Shobal, Zibeon, Anah, Dishon, Ezer, and Dishan, the dukes of the Horites. Deuteronomy 2:12 and 2:22 record that the children of Esau destroyed the Horites and dwelt in their stead, just as Israel would later do in Canaan.
Culture: Their name is traditionally connected with cave-dwelling in Seir's mountains. They were organized under dukes, a clan structure that Esau's line inherited along with the land.
Religion: No Horite religion is described in the text.
BibleConnection: The Horites show the pattern Deuteronomy repeats: one people displacing another in the land, so that Edom's story mirrors Israel's own conquest.

TimePeriod: Patriarchal era onward, c. 2000 BC and after
Region: The desert east of Egypt, from Havilah to Shur, and later the northern Arabian desert
History: The Ishmaelites descended from Ishmael, son of Abraham and Hagar (Genesis 16; 21). Genesis 25:12-18 lists his twelve sons, princes of their tribes, dwelling from Havilah to Shur, east of Egypt. An Ishmaelite caravan carrying spices to Egypt bought Joseph from his brothers (Genesis 37:25-28; the same passage also calls the traders Midianites, and the two names are used together there). Gideon asked for the gold earrings of the Ishmaelite traders after defeating Midian (Judges 8:24), and Psalm 83:6 counts the Ishmaelites among the confederates against Israel.
Culture: Nomadic desert traders, living in tents and moving goods between Arabia and Egypt. Ishmael himself 'grew, and dwelt in the wilderness, and became an archer' (Genesis 21:20).
Religion: The text ties Ishmael's line to Abraham's God through Hagar's encounter at the well (Genesis 16) and God's promise to make Ishmael a great nation (Genesis 17:20), but it describes no distinct Ishmaelite religion.
BibleConnection: Ishmaelites carry Joseph into Egypt, setting the exodus story in motion, and stand as the desert kin of Israel: Abraham's other son's line, blessed yet outside the covenant promise.
KeyScriptures: Genesis 16:11-12; Genesis 21:20-21; Genesis 25:12-18; Genesis 37:25-28; Judges 8:24; Psalm 83:6
RelatedPeople: Abraham; Hagar; Ishmael; Isaac; Jacob; Joseph, Son of Jacob
RelatedEvents: Joseph and His Brothers; Hagar and Ishmael

Region: The Jezreel Valley, south of Naphtali
History: Issachar was Jacob's ninth son, by Leah. Jacob blessed him as a strong donkey crouching between sheepfolds, a tribe that would bear burdens (Genesis 49:14-15). His allotment lay in the fertile Jezreel Valley, including Jezreel and Shunem. Issachar's princes fought with Deborah and Barak (Judges 5:15), and the tribe's later fame was for wisdom: the men of Issachar 'had understanding of the times, to know what Israel ought to do' (1 Chronicles 12:32). Issachar was deported with the northern kingdom.
Culture: Issachar's culture was agricultural: the rich valley soil made it one of Israel's breadbaskets, and its strength lay in farming and in counsel rather than in kings or judges.
Religion: Issachar shared Israel's worship of the LORD, with its religious life centred on the sanctuary and later the temple at Jerusalem.
BibleConnection: Issachar is remembered for discernment rather than power: a tribe that knew its times and counselled the nation, in contrast to the strong-man history of its neighbours.
RelatedPeople: Issachar; Jacob; Moses; Joshua; Tola, Son of Puah; Baasha, King of Israel

Region: Jerusalem (called Jebus) and its surroundings
History: The Jebusites were the pre-Israelite inhabitants of Jerusalem. Genesis 10:16 lists them among the sons of Canaan. In Judges 1:21 the Benjamites failed to drive them out of Jerusalem, and in Judges 19:10 the city is still called Jebus, a city of the Jebusites. David captured their stronghold, the strong hold of Zion, and made it his capital (2 Samuel 5:6-9). Later, Araunah the Jebusite sold David the threshingfloor on Mount Moriah where the altar was built (2 Samuel 24:18-25).
Culture: A fortified city people. Their stronghold on the hill later called Zion held out against Judah and Benjamin until David took it, and the city they built became the capital of Israel.
Religion: They shared the Canaanite religion of their neighbors. The Bible records no distinct Jebusite cult, only that their city and its threshingfloor passed into Israel's worship when David built an altar there.
BibleConnection: The Jebusites held the city that became Jerusalem. Their defeat gave David his capital, and Araunah's threshingfloor became the site of the future temple.
KeyScriptures: Genesis 10:16; Joshua 15:63; Judges 1:21; Judges 19:10; 2 Samuel 5:6-9; 2 Samuel 24:18-25
RelatedEvents: David Becomes King; The Twelve Spies and Israel's Unbelief

Region: Southern hill country, from Jerusalem to Beersheba
History: Judah was Jacob's fourth son by Leah, whose name means praise. Jacob's blessing gave Judah the sceptre and the ruler's staff (Genesis 49:10), and the tribe produced the house of David. Judah's allotment covered the southern hill country including Hebron and, later, Jerusalem. After Solomon's death Judah became the southern kingdom, with Jerusalem and the temple, and it outlasted the northern kingdom by over a century before Babylon destroyed Jerusalem in 586 BC. The returning exiles were largely Judahites, and from 'Judah' comes the name 'Jew'. Jesus was born of Judah, of David's line, in Bethlehem.
Culture: Judah's culture was centred on Jerusalem, the temple, and the Davidic court. Its towns included Hebron, Bethlehem, and Lachish, and its people were farmers, shepherds, and traders of the southern hills.
Religion: Judah's religion was temple religion: sacrifice, priesthood, and the festivals in Jerusalem, guarded by prophets who called kings and people back to the covenant. After the exile, Judah's community rebuilt temple worship and the law became central to Jewish life.
BibleConnection: Judah carries the Bible's central thread: the promise of a ruler from Judah runs from Genesis 49 through David to Jesus, called the Lion of the tribe of Judah in Revelation 5.
KeyScriptures: Genesis 29:35; Genesis 49:8-12; Numbers 2:3; Joshua 15:1; 2 Samuel 2:4; 1 Kings 12:16-20; 2 Kings 25:1-2; Matthew 1:2-3
RelatedPeople: Judah; Jacob; Caleb; Boaz; Ruth; Naomi; Elimelech; King David; King Solomon; Rehoboam; King Asa; King Jehoshaphat; King Hezekiah; King Josiah; Zerubbabel; Jesse; Othniel, Son of Kenaz; Amos; Micah
RelatedEvents: Judah and Tamar; David Becomes King; Building of Solomon's Temple; The Kingdom Divides; Fall of Jerusalem and the Exile
RelatedFinds: LMLK Jar-Handle Seals; Hezekiah's Tunnel and Siloam Inscription; Lachish Letters; Ketef Hinnom Silver Scrolls; Cyrus Cylinder

Region: The east (the name means 'easterners'); no territory is stated in the text
History: The Kadmonites are named only once in the Bible, in the land promise to Abram (Genesis 15:19), among the peoples of the land: Kenites, Kenizzites, Kadmonites, Hittites, Perizzites, Rephaim, Amorites, Canaanites, Girgashites, and Jebusites. Nothing more is recorded about them: no king, city, territory, or later mention appears anywhere in the text.
Culture: Unknown. Their name points east, and they are sometimes grouped with the 'children of the east' of the desert fringe, but the text itself says no more.
Religion: Unknown.
BibleConnection: The Kadmonites appear only in the promise itself: part of the land God pledged to Abram's descendants, named once and never heard from again.

Region: The Negev and the southern wilderness, associated with Midian and with Judah's southern border
History: The Kenites are named in the land promise of Genesis 15:19 and in Balaam's oracle, which pictures their nest set in the rock (Numbers 24:21). The children of the Kenite, Moses' father-in-law, went up with Judah into the wilderness of Judah (Judges 1:16), and Heber the Kenite had separated from the Kenites when his wife Jael killed Sisera (Judges 4:11, 17-22). Saul warned the Kenites to leave the Amalekites before his campaign, because they had shown kindness to Israel coming out of Egypt (1 Samuel 15:6). David shared spoil with the Kenites (1 Samuel 30:29), and 1 Chronicles 2:55 counts scribal families among the Kenites, including the house of Rechab, whose abstinent rule Jeremiah 35 praises.
Culture: The name is traditionally connected with metalworking (Hebrew qayin, 'smith'), and the Kenites lived as tent-dwellers on the desert fringe, at home among both Midian and Judah. The Rechabites kept Jonadab's rule: no wine, no houses, no sown fields.
Religion: Jethro's family acknowledged the LORD (Exodus 18), and the Rechabites' obedience to their ancestor's command is held up in Jeremiah 35 as a rebuke to Judah's disobedience.
BibleConnection: Kenites are Israel's desert friends: kin by marriage to Moses, allies who showed kindness at the exodus, and the people whose tent Jael's peg ended Sisera's army.
KeyScriptures: Genesis 15:19; Numbers 24:21; Judges 1:16; Judges 4:11; Judges 4:17-22; 1 Samuel 15:6; 1 Chronicles 2:55; Jeremiah 35:6-10

Region: Southern Canaan and the Negev, associated with Caleb's family
History: The Kenizzites are named in the land promise of Genesis 15:19 and nowhere else as a nation. Their fame comes through one man: Caleb, son of Jephunneh the Kenizzite (Numbers 32:12; Joshua 14:6), who followed the LORD fully and received Hebron as his inheritance. Though called a Kenizzite, Caleb was counted with the tribe of Judah. Kenaz, named in 1 Chronicles 4:13-15, belongs to the same family line, and Othniel son of Kenaz took Debir and became a judge.
Culture: Little is recorded beyond their place in the Genesis 15 list and Caleb's line. They appear as a southern clan absorbed into Judah rather than as a separate kingdom.
Religion: No distinct Kenizzite religion is described. Caleb's faithfulness is the family's mark in the text.
BibleConnection: Through Caleb the Kenizzite, this obscure people of the promise list produced one of Israel's great heroes of faith, the spy who believed God could give the land.

Region: No single territory; 48 cities scattered throughout Israel
History: Levi was Jacob's third son by Leah, and with Simeon he shared in the Shechem violence (Genesis 34). The tribe was set apart after the golden calf, when the Levites rallied to Moses (Exodus 32:26-29). Levi received no tribal territory; instead the Levites were given 48 cities scattered among the other tribes (Joshua 21) and lived from the tithes, serving the tabernacle and later the temple. Aaron's descendants were the priests; the other Levites assisted them. Moses, Aaron, and Miriam were all Levites. Korah's rebellion (Numbers 16) was a Levite challenge to Aaron's priesthood.
Culture: Levite culture was defined by service rather than land: teaching the law, assisting at sacrifices, singing and guarding the sanctuary, and living dispersed among the other tribes as their religious instructors.
Religion: The Levites embodied Israel's priestly religion: Aaron's sons offered the sacrifices, and the tribe as a whole maintained the sanctuary, taught the law, and modelled the claim that the LORD himself was their inheritance (Numbers 18:20).
BibleConnection: Levi's blessing in Deuteronomy 33 praises the tribe that taught God's law and kept his covenant. In the New Testament the Levites appear in the parable of the good Samaritan and in the temple service that frames Jesus' ministry.
KeyScriptures: Genesis 29:34; Genesis 49:5-7; Exodus 32:26-29; Numbers 3:5-13; Numbers 18:20-24; Joshua 21:1-3; Deuteronomy 33:8-11
RelatedPeople: Levi; Jacob; Moses; Aaron; Miriam; Eleazar; Phinehas; Ithamar; Nadab; Abihu; Eli; Samuel; John the Baptist
RelatedEvents: The Golden Calf; The Ten Commandments

Region: North Africa, west of Egypt
History: The Lubim, or Libyans, appear as warriors of the North African coast west of Egypt. They marched with Shishak against Rehoboam (2 Chronicles 12:3) and are named among Egypt's allies (2 Chronicles 16:8; Nahum 3:9). Ezekiel lists Libya among the peoples falling with Egypt (Ezekiel 30:5) and among Gog's allies (Ezekiel 38:5), and Libyans were present at Pentecost (Acts 2:10). The Lehabim of Genesis 10:13 are traditionally identified with these Libyans.
Culture: Libyans were semi-nomadic herders and warriors of the coastal tribes, serving as soldiers and charioteers in Egyptian and other Near Eastern armies.
Religion: Libyans shared much of Egypt's religious world, worshipping Libyan and Egyptian deities of the desert and the Nile valley.
BibleConnection: Libya's biblical role is chiefly as Egypt's western neighbor and ally, named in judgment oracles and, at Pentecost, among the nations hearing the gospel in their own tongue.
KeyScriptures: 2 Chronicles 12:3; 2 Chronicles 16:8; Nahum 3:9; Ezekiel 30:5; Ezekiel 38:5; Acts 2:10

Region: Interior Asia Minor (Lycaonia)
History: Lycaonia was an inland district of Asia Minor. Paul preached at Lystra and Derbe in Lycaonia, where the crowds, hearing him in their own language, cried out that the gods had come down in human form and tried to sacrifice to him and Barnabas.
Culture: Lycaonian speech survived alongside Greek in a rural, pastoral district.
Religion: Local Zeus and Hermes cults — the crowd took Barnabas for Zeus and Paul for Hermes — before the gospel reached them.
BibleConnection: The Lycaonians' reaction at Lystra, and Paul's stoning there and return, are the Lycaonians' main New Testament appearance.

Region: Both sides of the Jordan: central hill country west, and Bashan and Gilead east
History: Manasseh was Joseph's elder son, adopted by Jacob as a tribal ancestor alongside Ephraim (Genesis 48). The tribe was the only one besides Reuben and Gad to hold land on both sides of the Jordan: half settled the central hills west of the river, and half took Bashan and northern Gilead east of it (Joshua 17; Numbers 32:33-42). Gideon, who delivered Israel from Midian, was a Manassite of Abiezer (Judges 6:15), and the judge Jephthah was a Gileadite. Manasseh's eastern half was deported early by Assyria, and the western half fell with Samaria in 722 BC.
Culture: Manasseh's culture was split by the Jordan: hill farming in the west, and pastoral, frontier life in Bashan and Gilead in the east, where its warriors guarded Israel's northern border.
Religion: Manasseh shared Israel's worship of the LORD, with its religious life centred on the sanctuary at Shiloh and later the temple, though its eastern towns lived far from both.
BibleConnection: Manasseh's double territory made it a bridge tribe: its western half gave the north its heartland, its eastern half its frontier, and its Gideon gave Israel one of its greatest deliverers.
KeyScriptures: Genesis 41:51; Genesis 48:13-20; Numbers 26:28-34; Joshua 17:1-6; Numbers 32:33-42; Judges 6:15
RelatedPeople: Manasseh; Jacob; Joseph, Son of Jacob; Ephraim; Moses; Joshua; Gideon; Jephthah, Judge of Israel; Jair, the Gileadite; Zelophehad
RelatedEvents: Gideon's Victory over Midian; Fall of Samaria

Region: Mesopotamia, between the Tigris and Euphrates
History: Mesopotamia was the land between the rivers, Abraham's homeland. Dwellers in Mesopotamia are named among the hearers at Pentecost, and Stephen recalls God appearing to Abraham while he was still in Mesopotamia.
Culture: Ancient cities, Aramaic-speaking under Parthian rule, with a large Jewish diaspora.
Religion: Old Mesopotamian cults alongside a strong Jewish diaspora community.
BibleConnection: Named at Pentecost, and named again as Abraham's homeland in Stephen's speech.

TimePeriod: Patriarchal era through the judges, c. 2000-1100 BC
Region: East of the Gulf of Aqaba, the Sinai wilderness, and Transjordan (northwest Arabia)
History: The Midianites descended from Midian, son of Abraham and Keturah (Genesis 25:2). Moses fled to Midian after killing the Egyptian, married Zipporah, daughter of Jethro the priest of Midian, and met God at the burning bush there (Exodus 2-3). Midian joined Moab in hiring Balaam (Numbers 22) and in the Baal-peor affair (Numbers 25), for which Israel made war on Midian (Numbers 31). In Gideon's day the Midianites, with Amalek and the children of the east, oppressed Israel for seven years until Gideon's three hundred routed them (Judges 6-8).
Culture: Nomadic herders and caravan traders of the desert fringe, living in tents and moving with their flocks. Their caravans linked Arabia, Egypt, and Canaan, and their kings are named in the Gideon campaign (Oreb, Zeeb, Zebah, Zalmunna).
Religion: Midianite religion included Baal-peor, worshipped with Moab in Numbers 25. Yet Jethro, priest of Midian, is shown acknowledging the LORD and offering sacrifice with Moses and Aaron (Exodus 18).
BibleConnection: Midian is where Moses found refuge, a wife, and his calling; and where Gideon won his great victory. The Midianite caravan also carried Joseph toward Egypt (Genesis 37:28, where the traders are called both Midianites and Ishmaelites).
KeyScriptures: Genesis 25:2; Exodus 2:15-21; Exodus 18:1-12; Numbers 25:16-18; Numbers 31:1-12; Judges 6:1-6; Judges 7:19-25
RelatedPeople: Moses; Jethro; Hobab; Gideon; Midian; Keturah; Zipporah; Reuel
RelatedEvents: Gideon's Victory over Midian; Joseph and His Brothers; The Burning Bush

Region: Upper Galilee, west of the Jordan's sources
History: Naphtali was Jacob's sixth son, by Rachel's servant Bilhah. Jacob blessed him as a hind let loose (Genesis 49:21). His tribe settled the hills of Upper Galilee, around Kedesh. Barak, who defeated Sisera with Deborah, mustered his army from Naphtali (Judges 4:6), and Naphtali's men are praised for risking their lives in the battle (Judges 5:18). The tribe was among the first deported by Tiglath-Pileser of Assyria (2 Kings 15:29). Isaiah's promise that a light would dawn on 'the land of Naphtali' (Isaiah 9:1-2) is applied to Jesus' ministry in Galilee in Matthew 4.
Culture: Naphtali's culture was that of the Galilean hills: farming, herding, and the fortified towns of the north, on the frontier with Syria and Phoenicia.
Religion: Naphtali shared Israel's worship of the LORD, with its religious life centred on the sanctuary and later the temple, and its towns included Kedesh, a city of refuge.
BibleConnection: Naphtali links Deborah's victory to Jesus' ministry: the same northern hills where Barak fought are where Isaiah promised light and where Jesus began preaching.
KeyScriptures: Genesis 30:8; Genesis 49:21; Deuteronomy 33:23; Judges 4:6; Judges 5:18; 2 Kings 15:29; Isaiah 9:1-2; Matthew 4:13-16
RelatedPeople: Naphtali; Jacob; Deborah; Barak; Jael; Moses; Joshua

TimePeriod: Before the Flood, and again in the wilderness generation (as reported)
Region: No territory is given for them
History: The Nephilim are named twice. Genesis 6:4 says, 'There were giants in the earth in those days; and also after that, when the sons of God came in unto the daughters of men, and they bare children to them, the same became mighty men which were of old, men of renown.' Numbers 13:33 reports the spies' words: 'we saw the giants, the sons of Anak, which come of the giants: and we were in our own sight as grasshoppers.' Whether the Nephilim of Genesis 6 are the same as the Anakim of Numbers 13 is debated; this entry records both passages without merging them into a settled identification.
Culture: The text gives no culture for them beyond great stature and renown, set against the wickedness of the age before the Flood.
Religion: None is described. Their story belongs to the corruption that preceded the Flood, not to any nation's worship.
BibleConnection: The Nephilim frame the Bible's two great judgments on giants: the wickedness before the Flood, and the fear that nearly turned Israel back at the edge of the promised land.
RelatedEvents: The Twelve Spies and Israel's Unbelief

Region: Southern coast of Asia Minor (Pamphylia)
History: Pamphylia was the coastal plain of southern Asia Minor. Pamphylians are named among the hearers at Pentecost; Paul landed at Perga in Pamphylia on his first journey, and John Mark left the party there.
Culture: Greek coastal cities under Roman rule, with the temple of Artemis at Perga among their landmarks.
Religion: Pagan temples before conversion; Paul preached in the region on his first journey.
BibleConnection: Named among the Pentecost hearers; Paul's first journey passed through Pamphylia twice, landing at Perga and later returning through it.

Region: Persia and Mesopotamia east of Rome
History: Parthia was the Iranian empire east of Rome, its great eastern rival. Parthians are named among the hearers at Pentecost; the New Testament says nothing further about them.
Culture: A horse-archer aristocracy ruling a Greek-influenced administration across Persia and Mesopotamia.
Religion: Zoroastrian tradition alongside other cults of the empire.
BibleConnection: Named only in the Acts 2 list of peoples who heard the apostles at Pentecost.

TimePeriod: Patriarchal era through the conquest, c. 2000-1200 BC
Region: The hill country and open country of Canaan, especially around Shechem and Bethel
History: The Perizzites appear in the land from Abram's time: in Genesis 13:7 the Canaanite and the Perizzite already dwelt in the land when Abram and Lot separated. They are named in the promise of Genesis 15:20, in the exodus promise of Exodus 3:8, and among the seven nations of Deuteronomy 7:1. In Joshua 17:15 Joshua tells the house of Joseph to clear land in the hill country of the Perizzites and the Rephaim, and in Judges 1:4-5 Judah defeated the Perizzites at Bezek.
Culture: Their name is often connected with unwalled villages and open country, in contrast to the fortified cities of other Canaanite peoples. They lived alongside the Canaanites in the hill country rather than in one great city.
Religion: The text gives no distinct Perizzite religion; they are counted among the peoples whose idolatry Israel was told to reject.
BibleConnection: Perizzites stand in the background of the whole story, from Abram's arrival to the conquest: one of the peoples already in the land when God promised it, and one of the peoples Israel was told to displace.
KeyScriptures: Genesis 13:7; Genesis 15:20; Exodus 3:8; Deuteronomy 7:1; Joshua 17:15; Judges 1:4-5

Region: West-central Asia Minor (Phrygia)
History: Phrygia had been an ancient kingdom famed in legend for King Midas; by New Testament times it was part of the Roman province of Asia. Phrygians are named among the hearers at Pentecost, and Paul crossed Phrygia on his journeys.
Culture: Phrygian speech and the old mother-goddess cults were giving way to Greek language and Roman ways.
Religion: The mother-goddess cult before conversion; Christian communities grew along Paul's routes.
BibleConnection: Named among the Pentecost hearers; Paul passed through Phrygia and Galatia on his second journey and through Galatia and Phrygia on his third.

Region: Black Sea coast of Asia Minor (Pontus)
History: Pontus, on the southern Black Sea coast, had been a kingdom and was a Roman province by New Testament times. Pontians are named among the hearers at Pentecost, and Peter addresses his first letter to believers in Pontus.
Culture: Greek coastal cities with an inland population, under Roman administration.
Religion: Pagan cults before conversion; Christian communities existed there by the time of 1 Peter.
BibleConnection: Named among the Pentecost hearers; Aquila, Paul's fellow worker, was a native of Pontus; 1 Peter is addressed in part to Pontus.

Region: North Africa, west of Egypt (the Libya region)
History: Put, son of Ham (Genesis 10:6), is a North African people closely linked with the Libyans. The King James Version spells the name Phut in Genesis and Ezekiel and Put in Nahum. Put's warriors served in Tyre's army (Ezekiel 27:10), stood with Egypt's allies (Ezekiel 30:5; Nahum 3:9), and are named among Gog's coalition (Ezekiel 38:5). Beyond this warrior role, little is recorded of them.
Culture: Like their Libyan neighbors, the men of Put were known as soldiers and mercenaries in the armies of Tyre, Egypt, and the great powers.
Religion: Nothing distinct is recorded of Put's religion; as a North African people they shared the religious world of Libya and Egypt.
BibleConnection: Put appears only as a military ally in the prophets — with Tyre, with Egypt, and with Gog — a small people named wherever the great powers mustered their armies.

TimePeriod: Bronze Age, from Genesis 14 to David's reign
Region: Bashan (Og's kingdom), the Valley of Rephaim near Jerusalem, and Transjordan
History: The Rephaim were a people of great stature, remembered as giants. Chedorlaomer defeated them at Ashteroth Karnaim (Genesis 14:5), and they are named in the promise of Genesis 15:20. Deuteronomy 2 explains that the Emim and the Zamzummim were also accounted Rephaim, and that Og king of Bashan was 'of the remnant of the giants' (Deuteronomy 3:11), his iron bedstead kept at Rabbath as a curiosity. Joshua 12:4 and 13:12 record Og's kingdom as the last Rephaim territory, and David fought Philistines in the Valley of Rephaim (2 Samuel 5:18-22). Later Philistine giants (2 Samuel 21:16-22) are described as sons of Rapha, linking them to this giant tradition.
Culture: Remembered above all for their stature: 'a people great, and many, and tall' (Deuteronomy 2:10). They held kingdoms and valleys that Israel inherited piece by piece.
Religion: The text describes no Rephaim religion. In later biblical usage the same word shades into 'the shades' of the dead, but the people of Bashan and the valley are a nation, not a ghost story.
BibleConnection: The Rephaim are the giants of the conquest story: the fear behind the spies' report, the kingdom of Og that fell before Israel, and the valley where David fought for Jerusalem.
KeyScriptures: Genesis 14:5; Genesis 15:20; Deuteronomy 2:10-11; Deuteronomy 3:11; Joshua 12:4; 2 Samuel 5:18-22
RelatedPeople: Og; Abraham; Moses; King David; Joshua

Region: East of the Jordan, from the Arnon to Heshbon
History: Reuben was Jacob's firstborn, by Leah, but he lost the birthright after sleeping with his father's concubine Bilhah (Genesis 35:22; 49:3-4). At the settlement the tribe asked Moses for the pasture land east of the Jordan, on condition its fighting men cross over to help conquer Canaan (Numbers 32). Reubenites Dathan and Abiram joined Korah's rebellion against Moses (Numbers 16). The tribe was among the first carried away when Assyria overran the east-Jordan territory under Tiglath-Pileser (1 Chronicles 5:26).
Culture: Reuben shared the pastoral, tribal culture of Israel east of the Jordan, raising flocks on the Transjordan plateau. Its towns included Heshbon, a former Amorite capital, and its territory bordered Moab.
Religion: Reuben shared Israel's worship of the LORD, with its religious life centred on the tabernacle and later the temple at Jerusalem, despite living across the Jordan from them.
BibleConnection: Reuben's story is a warning about the firstborn's lost privilege: Jacob's blessing says Reuben was 'unstable as water' and would not excel. The tribe's request for land east of the Jordan set the pattern for the two and a half Transjordan tribes.
KeyScriptures: Genesis 29:32; Genesis 35:22; Genesis 49:3-4; Numbers 32:1-5; Joshua 13:15-23; Numbers 16:1
RelatedPeople: Reuben; Jacob; Moses; Aaron; Eleazar; Phinehas; Dathan; Abiram
RelatedEvents: The Exodus and the Red Sea; Crossing the Jordan

Region: Samaria, between Judea and Galilee
History: After Assyria conquered the northern kingdom, the population of Samaria mixed Israelite remnants with settlers from elsewhere in the empire. By New Testament times the Samaritans were a distinct people with their own temple on Mount Gerizim and a long, bitter estrangement from the Jews.
Culture: Samaritans kept the Torah (in their own Samaritan Pentateuch), observed the Sabbath and the feasts, and worshipped on Mount Gerizim rather than in Jerusalem.
Religion: Samaritan religion centred on the God of Israel, the Torah, Mount Gerizim as the chosen place of worship, and the expectation of a prophet like Moses (John 4:25).
BibleConnection: Jesus made a Samaritan the hero of his parable of neighbour-love, spoke at length with a Samaritan woman at Jacob's well, praised a Samaritan leper's thanks, and sent Philip to preach in Samaria, where Samaritans believed and received the Holy Spirit.
KeyScriptures: Matthew 10:5; Luke 10:33; Luke 17:16; John 4:9; Acts 8:25; 2 Kings 17:29; John 4:39

Region: Steppe north of the Black Sea
History: Scythians were the nomadic steppe peoples north of the Black Sea, proverbial outsiders in the Greek world. Paul names them once, as the far edge of the distinctions abolished in Christ.
Culture: Nomadic horsemen and famed archers, outside the Greek and Jewish worlds alike.
Religion: Steppe gods and customs, far from temple or synagogue.
BibleConnection: Named once, in Paul's list of distinctions — Greek and Jew, circumcised and uncircumcised, Barbarian, Scythian — that do not divide those renewed in Christ.

Region: Sepharvaim, on the Euphrates in Mesopotamia
History: The Sepharvites were one of the Mesopotamian peoples Assyria resettled in Samaria after Israel's fall (2 Kings 17:24). The Sepharvites burnt their children in fire to Adrammelech and Anammelech, the gods of Sepharvaim (2 Kings 17:31), and the kings of Sepharvaim were named by Assyria's king when he mocked the gods of the nations (2 Kings 18:34; 19:13).
Culture: As a Mesopotamian people, the Sepharvites shared the urban culture of the Euphrates cities.
Religion: The Sepharvites worshipped Adrammelech and Anammelech, to whom they offered child sacrifice — the Bible's darkest note on their religion.
BibleConnection: The Sepharvites stand in the Bible as a warning example twice over: a people whose gods could not save their cities from Assyria, and whose worship in Samaria showed how far the resettled land had fallen.

Region: The Negev within Judah's allotment, around Beersheba
History: Simeon was Jacob's second son by Leah. With his brother Levi he avenged Dinah by killing the men of Shechem (Genesis 34), and Jacob's blessing scattered both brothers in Israel (Genesis 49:5-7). Simeon's allotment lay inside Judah's territory in the south (Joshua 19:1-9), and the tribe was gradually absorbed into Judah; Simeonites are still named among those who joined Hezekiah's and Josiah's reforms (2 Chronicles 15:9; 34:6). By the second census the tribe had already shrunk sharply (Numbers 26:14).
Culture: Simeon shared Judah's southern, semi-pastoral culture, living in Negev towns such as Beersheba among Judah's settlements rather than as a separate territorial power.
Religion: Simeon shared Israel's worship of the LORD, with no separate cult or priesthood of its own; its towns fell under Judah's religious life centred on Jerusalem.
BibleConnection: Simeon's history illustrates Jacob's blessing fulfilled literally: a tribe scattered within Israel rather than holding its own land, yet still counted among the twelve and named in the sealing of Revelation 7.
RelatedPeople: Simeon; Jacob; Moses; Joshua; Zimri, Son of Salu; Shaul

Region: Canaan (location uncertain)
History: The Sinites are named once in the Table of Nations as descendants of Canaan (Genesis 10:17; 1 Chronicles 1:15), with no further biblical history. Later writers proposed locations from the northern Levant to farther east, but the text itself gives no location and no story, and none of those identifications is settled.
Culture: Nothing is recorded of Sinite culture apart from their place in the Canaanite family list.
Religion: Nothing distinct is recorded of Sinite religion; as Canaanites they belonged to the wider Canaanite world.
BibleConnection: The Sinites matter here only as part of the Bible's own map of the peoples: one branch of Canaan's family, named and then never heard from again.

Region: Phoenician coast under Syria
History: Syrophoenicia was the Phoenician coast as part of the Roman province of Syria. A Syrophoenician woman sought Jesus for her demon-possessed daughter, and he praised her faith; Mark names her people explicitly, 'a Greek, a Syrophenician by nation.'
Culture: Phoenician cities, Greek-speaking under Roman Syria.
Religion: Pagan background; the woman's persistence and faith are the story's point.
BibleConnection: Mark is the only Gospel to name this people, and he does so precisely to mark the woman as an outsider to Israel whose faith Jesus honoured.

Region: The land later held by Ammon, east of the Jordan
History: The Zamzummim were an ancient people of the Ammonite country, remembered as giants. Deuteronomy 2:20-21 says their land 'also was accounted a land of giants: giants dwelt therein in old time; and the Ammonites call them Zamzummim; a people great, and many, and tall, as the Anakims; but the LORD destroyed them before the Ammonites, and they succeeded them.' The Zuzim defeated at Ham in Genesis 14:5 are commonly identified with the Zamzummim, the same people under an older name.
Culture: Known only as a great and tall people, counted among the Rephaim, whose land passed to Ammon.
Religion: Not described in the text.
BibleConnection: Like the Emim, the Zamzummim teach Deuteronomy's point: God gave Ammon its land by displacing giants, just as He gave Israel Canaan.

Region: Lower Galilee, between the Jezreel Valley and the coast
History: Zebulun was Jacob's tenth son, by Leah. Jacob blessed him as a haven for ships (Genesis 49:13), though his allotment in Lower Galilee never quite reached the sea. Zebulun's men fought with Deborah and Barak and are praised for risking their lives on the heights (Judges 5:18); the tribe also supplied Elon, one of the minor judges (Judges 12:11-12). Isaiah's promise of light to Zebulun and Naphtali (Isaiah 9:1) is applied to Jesus' Galilean ministry in Matthew 4. Zebulun was deported with the northern kingdom.
Culture: Zebulun's culture was that of the Galilean farming towns, trading toward the coast and the great north-south road, with a reputation for loyalty in battle disproportionate to its size.
Religion: Zebulun shared Israel's worship of the LORD, with its religious life centred on the sanctuary and later the temple.
BibleConnection: Zebulun links the judges' battlefield to the Gospels: the tribe praised for risking its life at the Kishon is named in the same Isaiah promise that Matthew applies to Jesus in Galilee.
KeyScriptures: Genesis 30:20; Genesis 49:13; Deuteronomy 33:18-19; Joshua 19:10-16; Judges 5:14; Isaiah 9:1
RelatedPeople: Zebulun; Jacob; Moses; Joshua; Deborah; Barak; Elon, Judge of Israel

Region: Canaan (later Sumur on the Phoenician coast is the proposed identification)
History: The Zemarites are named in the Table of Nations as descendants of Canaan (Genesis 10:18; 1 Chronicles 1:16), with no further biblical history. The later coastal town of Sumur (Simyra) in the northern Levant has been proposed as their place, but the text itself does not say so, and the identification remains a proposal, not a certainty.
Culture: Nothing is recorded of Zemarite culture apart from their place in the Canaanite family list.
Religion: Nothing distinct is recorded of Zemarite religion.
BibleConnection: The Zemarites appear only in the Table of Nations, one branch of Canaan's family spread abroad.

TimePeriod: Ancient (Genesis 10 era); named again in Ezekiel 38
Region: The far north, in the company of Magog (Ezekiel 38:6); the precise location is debated
History: Gomer, son of Japheth, heads the first branch of the Table of Nations (Genesis 10:2). The name returns only in Ezekiel 38:6, where Gomer and his bands march in Gog's coalition from the north. Later writers commonly identify Gomer with the Cimmerians of the ancient Near East, but the text itself gives no location and no story, and that identification remains a proposal, not a certainty. Gomer the people is not Gomer the wife of Hosea, a different person.
Culture: Nothing distinct is recorded of Gomerite culture; in Ezekiel they appear only as a warrior host from the north.
Religion: Nothing distinct is recorded of Gomerite religion.
BibleConnection: Gomer brackets the Bible's north: a Japhethite name in the Table of Nations, then a northern invader in Ezekiel's oracle against Gog.

TimePeriod: Ancient (Genesis 10 era); Ezekiel's oracle and Revelation
Region: The far north (Ezekiel 38:2; 39:6); Magog is also named as a land, and a place entry covers the land sense
History: Magog, son of Japheth, is named in the Table of Nations (Genesis 10:2) and becomes the land of Gog's rule in Ezekiel 38-39: 'the land of Magog, the chief prince of Meshech and Tubal.' Ezekiel 39:6 sends fire on Magog itself. In Revelation 20:8 'Gog and Magog' gather for the final rebellion, an eschatological use of the names rather than a first-century nation. Gog is a ruler, not a people, and is not drafted here.
Culture: Nothing distinct is recorded of Magogite culture; in Ezekiel they appear as a great northern host.
Religion: Nothing distinct is recorded of Magogite religion.
BibleConnection: Magog moves from genealogy to prophecy: a Japhethite name, then the northern land of Ezekiel's invasion oracle, then the final rebellion's army in Revelation.

Region: The far north, paired with Tubal (Ezekiel 38:2); the precise location is debated, with an Anatolian and Black Sea region proposed
History: Meshech, son of Japheth, is named in the Table of Nations (Genesis 10:2). Psalm 120:5 makes Meshech proverbial for distant exile: 'Woe is me, that I sojourn in Mesech' (the Psalm spells the name Mesech). Ezekiel 27:13 has Meshech trading slaves and vessels of brass with Tyre, Ezekiel 32:26 counts Meshech among the slain nations gone down to the pit, and Ezekiel 38:2 puts Meshech under Gog's rule.
Culture: Traders in persons and bronze-work, in Ezekiel's Tyre catalogue (Ezekiel 27:13).
Religion: Nothing distinct is recorded of Meshechite religion.
BibleConnection: Meshech is the Bible's far north made personal: the psalmist's distant sojourn, Tyre's trading partner, and one of Gog's peoples.

Region: The far north, paired with Meshech (Ezekiel 38:2); the precise location is debated, with an Anatolian and Black Sea region proposed
History: Tubal, son of Japheth, is named in the Table of Nations (Genesis 10:2). Isaiah 66:19 sends messengers to Tubal and Javan among 'the isles afar off, that have not heard my fame.' Ezekiel 27:13 pairs Tubal with Meshech trading slaves and brass with Tyre, Ezekiel 32:26 counts Tubal among the slain nations, and Ezekiel 38:2 puts Tubal under Gog's rule.
Culture: Traders in persons and bronze-work, in Ezekiel's Tyre catalogue (Ezekiel 27:13).
Religion: Nothing distinct is recorded of Tubalite religion.
BibleConnection: Tubal stands with Meshech throughout: a Japhethite name, a distant coastland in Isaiah's mission vision, and one of Gog's peoples.

Region: The far north, 'of the north quarters' (Ezekiel 38:6); later writers link the name with Armenia, a proposal, not a certainty
History: Togarmah, son of Gomer, is named in the Table of Nations (Genesis 10:3). Ezekiel 27:14 has the house of Togarmah trading horses, horsemen, and mules with Tyre, and Ezekiel 38:6 marches Togarmah in Gog's coalition from the north quarters.
Culture: Horse-breeders and traders, in Ezekiel's Tyre catalogue (Ezekiel 27:14).
Religion: Nothing distinct is recorded of Togarmahite religion.
BibleConnection: Togarmah is the Bible's horse-supplier from the north: Tyre's market partner, then one of Gog's bands.

TimePeriod: Ancient (Genesis 10 era); Jeremiah's oracle against Babylon
Region: A northern kingdom summoned against Babylon (Jeremiah 51:27); the precise location is debated
History: Ashkenaz, son of Gomer, is named in the Table of Nations (Genesis 10:3). The name returns once, in Jeremiah 51:27, where the kingdoms of Ararat, Minni, and Ashchenaz are called together against Babylon (Jeremiah spells the name Ashchenaz). The later Jewish association of Ashkenaz with Germany belongs to a much later period and is not the biblical identification.
Culture: Nothing distinct is recorded of Ashkenazite culture beyond a kingdom able to answer Jeremiah's summons.
Religion: Nothing distinct is recorded of Ashkenazite religion.
BibleConnection: Ashkenaz appears twice: a Gomerite name in the Table of Nations, then a northern kingdom in Jeremiah's oracle of Babylon's fall.

Region: A Cushite kingdom, named beside Egypt and Ethiopia (Isaiah 43:3); the precise location is debated, with an upper Nile region proposed
History: Seba, son of Cush, is named in the Table of Nations (Genesis 10:7). Psalm 72:10 has the kings of Sheba and Seba offering gifts, treating them as two distinct kingdoms. Isaiah 43:3 gives 'Ethiopia and Seba' as Israel's ransom, and Isaiah 45:14 names 'the Sabeans, men of stature' among the peoples coming over to Israel. Seba is not Sheba: the two names sit side by side in Psalm 72:10 and belong to different lines, Seba to Cush and Sheba to Raamah and to Joktan.
Culture: A trading kingdom of the south, named for its merchandise in Isaiah 45:14.
Religion: Nothing distinct is recorded of Sebaite religion.
BibleConnection: Seba is the southern kingdom in Israel's ransom price and tribute vision: named with Egypt and Ethiopia, distinct from Sheba.

Region: The western sea-peoples: 'ships of Chittim' (Numbers 24:24; Daniel 11:30); usually identified with Cyprus and the western Mediterranean islands, an identification, not a certainty
History: Chittim, son of Javan, is named in the Table of Nations (Genesis 10:4). Balaam's oracle warns that 'ships shall come from the coast of Chittim' and afflict both Asshur and Eber (Numbers 24:24). Isaiah 23:1 and 23:12 tie Chittim to Tyre's shipping news, Jeremiah 2:10 sends Israel to 'pass over the isles of Chittim' and see, Ezekiel 27:6 brings ivory 'out of the isles of Chittim,' and Daniel 11:30 has 'ships of Chittim' turning back the king of the north. Modern scholarship usually spells the name Kittim.
Culture: Seafarers and traders of the western isles, in Tyre's orbit.
Religion: Nothing distinct is recorded of Chittimite religion.
BibleConnection: Chittim is the Bible's west: the ships that come from beyond the sea in Balaam's oracle, Isaiah's Tyre lament, and Daniel's wars.
KeyScriptures: Numbers 24:24; Isaiah 23:1; Isaiah 23:12; Jeremiah 2:10; Ezekiel 27:6; Daniel 11:30

TimePeriod: 9th-6th centuries BC (Neo-Babylonian ascendancy); the name also survives as a learned caste in Daniel
Region: Southern Mesopotamia, centred on Babylon
History: The Chaldeans are the people of Chaldea who rose under Nabopolassar and Nebuchadnezzar to rule the Neo-Babylonian empire. Habakkuk 1:6 calls them 'that bitter and hasty nation, which shall march through the breadth of the land, to possess the dwellingplaces that are not theirs.' Jeremiah names them as the besiegers of Jerusalem again and again (Jeremiah 21:4), and Job 1:17 has Chaldean raiders carrying off Job's camels. In Daniel the same word also denotes a learned caste: the 'tongue of the Chaldeans' (Daniel 1:4) and the Chaldeans summoned as wise men and astrologers (Daniel 2:2). Both uses are kept distinct here: the nation and the caste. Note on placement: the October 27 civilizations merge deliberately folded Chaldeans into the Babylon entry; this draft treats the people and the caste distinctly from the empire, and publishing it reverses that fold without touching the Babylon entry.
Culture: Imperial administrators, soldiers, and scholars: the ruling people of Nebuchadnezzar's Babylon, and in Daniel a caste of astrologers and wise men.
Religion: The gods of Babylon, including Bel and Nebo; in Daniel the Chaldeans serve as the court diviners whose wisdom Daniel's God surpasses.
BibleConnection: The Chaldeans are the instrument of Judah's exile in Jeremiah and Habakkuk, the raiders of Job's prologue, and the court wise men of Daniel.
RelatedEvents: Fall of Jerusalem and the Exile
RelatedFinds: Babylonian Chronicle (Nebuchadnezzar's Chronicle); Nebuchadnezzar II Babylon City Wall Cylinder

TimePeriod: From Genesis through the prophets (Arabian nomad horizon)
Region: The Arabian desert east of Israel, in tents and villages (Isaiah 42:11; Psalm 120:5)
History: Kedar, son of Ishmael, heads the Arabian nomads of the prophets. Psalm 120:5 makes 'the tents of Kedar' proverbial for distant dwelling, and the Song of Songs borrows the same image for dark tents (Song of Songs 1:5). Isaiah 21:16-17 gives Kedar's glory a single year to fail, Isaiah 42:11 calls the villages that Kedar inhabits to sing, Isaiah 60:7 gathers 'the flocks of Kedar' to the restored Zion, Jeremiah 49:28 sends Nebuchadnezzar against Kedar's men of the east, and Ezekiel 27:21 has Arabia and the princes of Kedar trading lambs, rams, and goats with Tyre.
Culture: Nomadic herders of the Arabian desert, living in tents and villages, trading flocks with Tyre.
Religion: Nothing distinct is recorded of Kedarite religion.
BibleConnection: Kedar is the desert neighbor in Israel's poetry and prophecy: the psalmist's distant tent, Isaiah's doomed glory and gathered flock, Jeremiah's target.
KeyScriptures: Genesis 25:13; Psalm 120:5; Isaiah 21:16; Isaiah 42:11; Isaiah 60:7; Jeremiah 49:28; Ezekiel 27:21

TimePeriod: Patriarchal era (Genesis) and Isaiah's restoration vision
Region: Arabian, beside Kedar (Isaiah 60:7); the precise location is not stated
History: Nebaioth, firstborn of Ishmael, is named in the Ishmaelite list (Genesis 25:13). Esau married Mahalath, daughter of Ishmael and sister of Nebajoth (Genesis 28:9; 36:3 spells the name Nebajoth), tying Nebaioth's house to Esau's line. The name returns in Isaiah 60:7, where 'the rams of Nebaioth shall minister unto thee' at the restored Zion, beside the flocks of Kedar.
Culture: Herders of the Arabian desert, named for their rams in Isaiah's vision.
Religion: Nothing distinct is recorded of Nebaiothite religion.
BibleConnection: Nebaioth links Ishmael's firstborn to Esau's household and to Isaiah's gathered flocks.

Region: East of Gilead (1 Chronicles 5:10); the Reubenites, Gadites, and half-tribe of Manasseh took their land
History: The Hagarites are the Arabian people fought by Reuben, Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh east of Gilead (1 Chronicles 5:10). In the fuller war account they fight alongside Jetur, Nephish, and Nodab, and are defeated because their enemies 'cried to God in the battle' (1 Chronicles 5:19-20). Psalm 83:6 names the 'Hagarenes' in the confederacy against Israel. The name is traditionally taken from Hagar, but the text itself does not state the descent, and the tradition is noted as tradition. Modern works usually spell the name Hagrites.
Culture: An eastern people with tents and livestock, taken in war by the Transjordan tribes.
Religion: Nothing distinct is recorded of Hagarite religion.
BibleConnection: The Hagarites are the eastern enemy of the Transjordan tribes: defeated in a war the Chronicler credits to prayer, then named in Psalm 83's confederacy.

TimePeriod: From Deuteronomy through Ezekiel (Late Bronze Age to exile)
Region: The Phoenician coast around Sidon, north of Tyre
History: Sidon was Canaan's firstborn (Genesis 10:15), and the Sidonians are the distinct city-people of Sidon, not Phoenicians in general: the Phoenicia entry covers Phoenicians broadly, while this entry covers Sidon itself, on the same pattern as Samaritans beside Samaria. Deuteronomy 3:9 notes that the Sidonians call Hermon Sirion. Judges 3:3 and 10:12 count Sidonians among Israel's oppressors, and Judges 18:7 describes the Zidonians as 'quiet and secure.' Solomon hired Sidonians as skilled timbermen for the temple (1 Kings 5:6), then married Sidonian wives and followed Ashtoreth, goddess of the Zidonians (1 Kings 11:1, 33). Jezebel was the daughter of Ethbaal, king of the Zidonians (1 Kings 16:31). Ezekiel 32:30 counts the Zidonians among the slain gone down to the pit. The King James Version uses both Sidonians and Zidonians for this people.
Culture: Seafarers and timbermen of the Phoenician coast, famed for cedar work and trade.
Religion: Ashtoreth, goddess of the Zidonians, carried into Israel by Solomon's Sidonian wives and by Jezebel.
BibleConnection: Sidonians touch Israel at every turn: oppressors in Judges, temple workmen under Solomon, the source of Jezebel, and the slain of Ezekiel.
KeyScriptures: Deuteronomy 3:9; Judges 3:3; Judges 10:12; Judges 18:7; 1 Kings 5:6; 1 Kings 11:1; Ezekiel 32:30

Region: Northwest Arabia, on the incense-trade routes; the precise site is debated, with the oasis of al-Ula the usual proposal
History: Two Dedans appear in Genesis and must not be merged silently: Dedan son of Raamah (Genesis 10:7) and Dedan son of Jokshan (Genesis 25:3). The Arabian traders of the prophets are Dedan without further distinction in the text. Jeremiah 25:23 names Dedan among the judged nations, Jeremiah 49:8 warns the inhabitants of Dedan to flee and dwell deep, Ezekiel 27:15 and 27:20 have Dedan trading ivory, ebony, and saddlecloths with Tyre, and Ezekiel 38:13 has Sheba and Dedan questioning Gog's spoil.
Culture: Caravan traders of northwest Arabia, dealing in ivory, ebony, and fine cloth.
Religion: Nothing distinct is recorded of Dedanite religion.
BibleConnection: Dedan is the Arabian merchant in Tyre's market, the warned inhabitant of Jeremiah's oracle, and the questioner of Gog's spoil.
KeyScriptures: Genesis 10:7; Genesis 25:3; Jeremiah 25:23; Jeremiah 49:8; Ezekiel 27:15; Ezekiel 27:20; Ezekiel 38:13

TimePeriod: Patriarchal era through the monarchy; the name still appears in the Gospels (Matthew 15:22)
Region: The land of Canaan, from Sidon to Gaza and inland to the Jordan (Genesis 10:19)
History: This entry covers the Canaanites as a people; the land and its city-states are covered by the Canaan entry in Civilizations. The Canaanites descend from Canaan, son of Ham (Genesis 10:15-19), whose sons give the coastal and inland peoples their names. The name is sometimes used broadly for all the pre-Israelite inhabitants: 'the Canaanite was then in the land' when Abram arrived (Genesis 12:6). Deuteronomy 7:1 counts the Canaanites among the seven nations Israel was to displace, and Joshua 3:10 names them among the peoples the living God would drive out. In Judges the pattern reverses: Israel 'dwelt among the Canaanites' and took their daughters in marriage (Judges 3:5), and the peoples and their gods became the standing test of the covenant.
Culture: City-dwellers and farmers of walled towns and open villages, trading along the coastal road and the Jordan Valley.
Religion: The gods of Canaan, Baal and Asherah and the gods of the city-states, whose worship Israel was warned against and repeatedly adopted.
BibleConnection: The Canaanites are the peoples of the Promised Land: the inhabitants Israel was told to displace, the neighbors Israel lived among, and the constant covenant test of Judges.
RelatedEvents: The Twelve Spies and Israel's Unbelief; The Walls of Jericho

TimePeriod: c. 1200-600 BC (settlement to the Babylonian period); named already in Genesis
Region: The southern coastal plain: Gaza, Ashkelon, Ashdod, Ekron, Gath
History: This entry covers the Philistines as a people; the five-city league and its wars as a polity are covered by the Philistia entry in Civilizations. The Philistines are usually identified with the Peleset of the Egyptian Sea Peoples records, who settled the southern coast around 1200 BC, but that identification is a scholarly proposal, not a certainty. Genesis already names Philistines in Abraham's day (Genesis 21:34), before the Sea Peoples settlement, a point scholars debate, whether as an early presence or a later name applied backward. In the judges era they oppressed Israel (Judges 13:1) and Samson fought them single-handed; they captured the ark and set it in Dagon's temple before returning it (1 Samuel 5:1). Goliath of Gath challenged Israel's army (1 Samuel 17:1), and David fought them as outlaw, king, and old man (2 Samuel 5:17). Amos 9:7 traces them to Caphtor. Under the empires that followed, the Philistine cities were absorbed and the people disappear from the record.
Culture: Aegean settlers turned coastal city-dwellers, famed for iron-working and for the bichrome pottery that marks their towns; their five cities shared a league but kept their own lords.
Religion: Dagon, god of Ashdod, and Ashtaroth, goddess of the Philistine cities; the ark stood in Dagon's temple before it was returned.
BibleConnection: The Philistines are Israel's great early rival: Samson's enemy, the captors of the ark, Goliath's people, and the power David fought before and after becoming king.
KeyScriptures: Genesis 21:34; Judges 13:1; 1 Samuel 5:1; 1 Samuel 17:1; 2 Samuel 5:17; Amos 9:7
RelatedPeople: Samson; Delilah; Goliath; King Saul; King David
RelatedEvents: David and Goliath; Samson and Delilah
RelatedFinds: Ekron Temple Inscription; Philistine Bichrome Pottery; Sargon II Ashdod Stele Fragments

TimePeriod: c. 1500-300 BC, with a New Testament presence in the Gospels
Region: The northern Levantine coast around Tyre and Sidon, with colonies across the Mediterranean
